results.title: Performance, Stress, and Load Tests in Rails | AppSignal Blog
results.content: # Performance, Stress, and Load Tests in Rails. Tests are an integral part of most well-working Rails applications where maintenance isn't a nightmare and new features are consistently added, or existing ones are improved. Thankfully, Rails has good support not only for unit, end-to-end, and integration tests but also for tests related to performance and loading. I’ll cover all of them in the article and show some practical examples that will help you understand how to efficiently use tools that test the performance level of your application. * **Theoretical** — I'll show you why testing is necessary, the kinds of tests we can perform and the metrics that are essential when performing tests on an application. * **Practical** — we'll get our hands dirty and write tests for an actual application to get the output. After reading the two sections, you'll have a deeper understanding of the different types of tests and how to perform them on your Rails application. There are three primary types of tests that you can write to ensure that your Rails application’s performance is correct and the infrastructure is working well under the heavy workload. The primary purpose of such tests is to get a specific set of metrics on which base we can take some action to improve the application’s code. That being said, we are now prepared to move to the last step of the theory part: learning what metrics are essential when doing performance testing on a Rails application. That’s why the first step in the practice part is to write a simple Rails application that we can write the tests for. Let’s walk step-by-step through a simple test configuration to simulate a single user request to the main page of the simple app we created before. After performing the load test, you'll know the pain points of your application. Understanding the user limit, you can now perform the stress test to see how the application will behave. ## Performance Tests With Ruby-prof. The performance test feature was built-in in Rails until version 3, and then it was extracted to the separate gem . * the way you can test the performance of your Rails app.

results.title: How to Simulate Ecommerce Traffic Patterns in Load Tests
results.content: # How to Simulate Ecommerce Traffic Patterns in Load Tests. If you simply point a load testing tool at checkout and hit “start,” you miss 90% of what users are really doing. We’ll cover the unique characteristics of ecommerce traffic, practical ways to model flows like browsing and purchasing in the right proportions, common mistakes that undermine realism, and best practices that elevate your tests from generic stress checks to business-relevant insights. When creating load test scenarios, it’s a good idea to think beyond “all users checkout.” Because as we know, *most users don’t checkout.* Instead, you should capture the spectrum of ecommerce user behaviors. In aggregate, this is the heaviest load on your content delivery, caching, and catalog APIs. Browsing traffic stresses read-heavy parts of the stack and reveals where CDNs, caching layers, or slow database queries can bottleneck. Search heavy sessions are unique in load testing. Simulating this traffic matters because it stresses cart persistence, session storage, and database writes, even though the user never completes checkout. If your load test models only successful purchases, you overlook a major category of real traffic. Load testing this flow validates revenue-critical infrastructure. This ensures browsing remains the dominant load driver while checkout is tested proportionally. Load tests that ignore this distribution miss CDN latency issues, mobile-specific performance problems, and regional gateway bottleneck. Designing a load test for ecommerce isn’t just about throwing traffic at the system—it’s about shaping that traffic to resemble real users as closely as possible. Even well-intentioned load tests can miss the mark if they don’t reflect how ecommerce systems actually behave under pressure. Modeling 100% buyers inflates checkout testing and ignores real browsing load. ## Example Ecommerce Load Testing Scenarios. Stresses product search, category browsing, and recommendation APIs. Realistic weekday flows often highlight caching misconfigurations that don’t show up in checkout-only tests. This transforms load testing from brute-force HTTP flooding to user-journey simulation. Load testing ecommerce is not about load times under stress bragging rights—it’s about realism. If you simulate traffic that doesn’t match your users, you test the wrong bottlenecks, fix the wrong problems, and risk failure when it matters most.
